# Log prose feedback

Read each complete log in Potato. Add notes about the writing in **Notes**.
Quote the passage or name its section. Use **Add note** to save each memo.
Use the optional whole-log comment field for general feedback. Tell AL when done;
stop the review server before import.

## Scope

All three current `logs/*.md` files are agent-written operational logs:

1. Two collections, one archive
2. Using Autolith so far
3. Orchestrating Autolith for a personal laboratory

The [authoring guide](../writing.md#start-a-post) assigns logs to the agent and
meditations to raj. The first log also states this distinction in **Different
authors**. The other two logs record agent work on Autolith. No meditations are
included.

Each item shows its title and the complete, unchanged Markdown snapshot in an
expanded text field. Section headings, code, diagrams, links, and front matter
are preserved. Notes belong to that exact log item. The post hashes above identify
the reviewed versions.

This pass collects prose feedback. It does not request term or link decisions,
advance a post state, or approve commit or publication. Preserve existing review
history and wait for raj's feedback before refining writing policy.

## Open and import

Queue with `just queue-review docs/reviews/log-memos-2026-11-21.md`.
Run `just review` and open http://127.0.0.1:8768/.

After raj finishes, import with `just import-reviews ID`, using the queued session
ID. Read the native comments, memos, and memo threads against the frozen text.
Review changed-source flags before using the feedback.

---
title: Two collections, one archive
date: 2026-10-06T10:54:12Z
---

# Abstract

This log explains why raj keeps records of agent work separate from personal meditations. Both collections use one archive.

# Context

raj wants a record of work that agents do at raj's request. The blog already holds raj's personal writing. The work records need to remain available without becoming part of that writing.

# Different authors

raj writes meditations. Agents write logs when raj asks for a record. The separate collections make this difference clear.

A log explains the reason for a task, the action, and the result or expected change. A meditation can contain personal thoughts without following that format.

# One place to find entries

Separate collections do not need separate search systems. The same index, search, and map include both collections. raj can find entries about a subject across both collections, then use a collection filter to limit the view.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  accTitle: Separate authors, one archive
  accDescr: raj writes meditations. Agents write logs at raj's request. Both collections enter the shared archive.
  R[raj] --> M[Meditations]
  R -->|Requests a record| A[Agents]
  A --> L[Logs]
  M --> S[Shared archive]
  L --> S
```

# Clear source labels

The index uses `mx` codes for meditations and `lx` codes for logs. Each collection has its own number sequence. The map uses filled points for meditations and outlined points for logs. These signs keep the source clear when both collections appear together.

# Review before publication

Each log has only a title and date before the text. Links can connect a log to earlier meditations and blogs.

raj can review and revise a local draft before asking for a commit. A revision does not approve a commit. A commit does not approve publication.

# Conclusion

raj can keep a record of agent work without changing the purpose of meditations. Both remain easy to find in one archive.

---
title: Using Autolith so far
date: 2026-10-07T03:52:29Z
---

# Abstract

raj has started to use Autolith for local setup and blog work. This log records the Lisp environment, shared settings, development checkout, and writing workflow established so far.

# Context

raj spent about half a day exploring Autolith on a Fedora VPS. Autolith runs in a live Common Lisp image. It provides a place to work with code, files, and processes through conversation.

raj's meditation, "the lisp machine," records the personal reason for this work. raj wants to return to Lisp and develop side projects. This log records the concrete setup and its current limits.

# A Lisp environment on the VPS

raj chose the ncurses build of Lem instead of Emacs for Lisp editing. The Lem setup includes Vim bindings. Shared settings live in the dotfiles repository and load from a Common Lisp init file.

This provides a terminal editor beside Autolith. The editor settings can be installed again without copying local history or generated files.

# Shared Autolith settings

raj added an Autolith package to the dotfiles repository. Its init file sets the model, reasoning effort, reasoning traces, and Simple Technical English. A separate local init file can supply machine-specific settings.

The shared package records the intended setup. Credentials, conversations, caches, and other runtime state stay outside that package. This separates portable configuration from the state of one machine.

# A separate development checkout

raj created a fork of Autolith and a local development checkout. The checkout has raj's fork as its origin and the original project as its upstream.

The development checkout is separate from the installed Autolith release. It is also separate from private changes to the running image. This gives raj a place for future source changes without treating local setup as a change to the project. This log does not record a new Autolith source feature.

# Preparing the blog for local work

raj used Autolith to prepare the blog's local embedding and build environment. The setup uses a separate Python environment for inference and Node.js for the site assets. Local checks covered embedding freshness, the site build, and the Python and JavaScript tests.

Markdown is the source of each post. The [embedding updater](/embeddings/) stores archive state in blog.sqlite. The site builder produces the local site, search index, and shared map.

During the setup checks, existing entries reused their stored vectors. Those checks verified the local workflow, but did not exercise a new model download or new inference.

# Bringing the log rules into Autolith

raj already used the ops-log skill in OMP to write operational logs. Before installing that skill in Autolith, raj asked for a review of the skill and the blog workflow.

The Autolith version keeps the same writing rules. Logs explain raj's work and intent. They use title and date front matter, an Abstract, Context, named sections, a Conclusion, and links to relevant past posts. New prose uses Simplified Technical English. Short sentences must still contain the material decisions and results.

The skill also tells Autolith where to start: the local blog checkout. Autolith must read the current README, check existing posts, preserve unrelated changes, and verify the local preview.

# Installing the skill as a regular file

The installed skill is a regular-file copy inside Autolith's configuration directory. The dotfiles package excludes skills from Stow and documents the copy step. Autolith lists ops-log in its skill catalog.

After a change to the tracked skill, the installed copy needs an update.

# Review before commit and publication

raj keeps personal meditations separate from agent-written logs. Both collections use [the same archive, search, and map](/logs/2026-10-06-two-collections-one-archive/). A log does not authorize an edit to raj's meditation prose.

A request for a draft starts local iteration. Autolith updates the embedding state and builds a preview for review. A revision does not approve a commit. A commit request does not approve a push or publication.

The copied skill records these boundaries. This draft is the first local log written with that Autolith setup.

# Conclusion

raj now has a local Lisp editor, shared Autolith settings, a separate development checkout, and a working blog setup. Autolith can use the existing operational log rules when raj requests a record of work.

This is an initial setup, not a report of completed side projects or new Autolith features. raj can refine the workflow through further use. The current log is a local draft for review.

---
title: Orchestrating Autolith for a personal laboratory
date: 2026-11-06T10:17:50+05:30
---

# Abstract

raj is experimenting with personal swarms of agents. He wants persistent project contexts, direct communication between agents, and clear control over work across machines. He is moving toward Autolith after trying a mixed set of agent systems.

Local agents already communicate and keep separate contexts. The proposed cross-machine system still needs trials. Its purpose is to support a personal computer science laboratory, with reproducible experiments, useful records, blogs, and eventually papers.

# Context

raj read David J. Moore's [A Taxonomy of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems: Design Patterns, Coordination Mechanisms, and Industrial Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12683). Hierarchical multi-agent systems (HMAS) organize agents in layers. He is considering how to apply those ideas to personal work.

He tried Paperclip on a NixOS virtual private server, Hermes on a ThinkPad, and Autolith on a Mac. He now prefers Autolith heads across machines instead of this mixed setup. A head is the agent responsible for execution and resources on one machine.

Orch verified removal of the Paperclip and Hermes services from their active system configurations. The former services and endpoints are inactive. Data and rollback state were retained. The running and boot system profiles match on both machines, but reboot behavior was not tested.

The ThinkPad already had Autolith before this change. No replacement Autolith was installed on the virtual private server. The proposed organization of machine heads still needs implementation and tests. Removing the old services does not establish a working cluster.

# Separate contexts and one task owner

Persistent project agents keep the context for their own projects. They can communicate directly instead of requiring raj to repeat each report. Persistence means that an agent can resume its work. It does not require continuous inference.

Orch is the coordinating agent. It handles priorities across projects and requests for raj's attention. Machine heads manage local execution and resource conflicts. Project agents retain domain knowledge. One agent must own each task, even when other agents contribute.

raj is considering a shallow hierarchy. For example, Orch could also act as the Mac head at first. Adding machines should not require adding layers of coordination to every small task.

The current local workflow already includes separate project contexts and direct agent messages. Extending that workflow across machines needs separate transport, recovery, and permission checks. Local success does not prove remote readiness.

# Match the method to the work

Use direct tools for small, exact tasks. A command, file read, or calculation often needs no additional agent.

For independent work, use low-effort workers for clear, bounded tasks with explicit checks. Use medium-effort workers for implementation, debugging, unclear scope, or failed checks. Keep the main coordinator at medium effort unless raj chooses otherwise.

The reason is practical: delegation adds context transfer and review. Use it when independent work can improve the result or reduce elapsed time. More agents do not, by themselves, produce better research. More machines also do not multiply a shared provider quota.

Native Lisp peer discovery gives local agents structured session information. They can resolve a current peer without parsing a terminal status report. This identifies a local destination. It does not establish remote discovery or grant permission to act.

Shared files also do not prove shared runtime state. Two agents can read the same configuration while running different loaded definitions. Changes need an appropriate reload and a check of the active state.

# Make work resumable across machines

The proposed system needs a record for each task. That record should identify the objective, owner, machine, workspace, input revisions, permitted actions, budget, output location, and completion check.

Keep task identity separate from a running process. After a restart, an agent should recover its commitments and next permitted step. It should inspect existing jobs before starting replacements. An inactive agent context should use no inference budget.

Delivery, acceptance, execution, and verified completion are different states. A sent message is not proof that work finished. Keep results until the receiving agent acknowledges them.

Disconnects make retries difficult. If a reply is missing, inspect the actual state before repeating an action with side effects. Identify duplicate requests and bound the number of retries. For cancellation, check that the underlying jobs and child agents stopped.

These are requirements for the cross-machine design. They are not claims that remote recovery and cancellation have passed tests.

# Evaluate research, not agent activity

The long-term goal is a [personal computer science laboratory](/laboratory/). The cluster is one application within it. More messages or completed subtasks are weak evidence of research progress.

For an investigation, retain the question, code and input versions, environment, configuration, measurements, and uncertainty. Preserve negative results. Separate exploration from reproduction and review. A model's claim is not a measurement.

A useful first remote trial would produce a read-only artifact that another agent can check independently. Later trials should cover disconnects, duplicate delivery, restart, and cancellation. An isolated write task needs its own permission. Complete a real investigation before expanding the system.

Research output should pass verification before it reaches the blog or a paper.

# Conclusion

raj has chosen a direction: persistent Autolith agents with separate project contexts, direct communication, and a shallow structure for coordination. The local workflow provides a starting point. The proposed cross-machine system still needs verified transport, bounded tasks, recovery tests, and a first reproducible investigation.

memos.body: we should go for more of a we vibe instead of "raj" (I) and you being separate entities - again think of this as more of a laboratory publishing kinda vibe.

title is dry - not my style - something like - "autolith'ing" or "on autolith" or something more my style would be nice. should take a look at my titles from my old blog - https://github.com/rajp152k/23-26_archive  to build a taste for what kind of writing is more natural to me.
do refer to generically applicable notes give to the "two collections, one archive" log

yeah - we should consider identifying apportunities to use mermaid whenever possible - it should not be forced. but we should have diagrams where it aids the comprehension of the reader - for instance - right now ; there could be graph denoting all the computers, the topology being followed, with a human to represent me in the loop whenever i do come in (i don't know if mermaid allows graphs in the sense of edges and nodes - might consider another candidate for this kind of stuff - something that is mathematically more capable rather than just swe based stuff)
the conclusion is forced - it's not doing anything new - we could get rid of it. actually this evals process that we're going through now should help us build a really native style down the line.
do refer to the generic notes for the other blogs. refine and i'll review this again later on.

both collections use one archive - is that really necessary? more of a factoid that does not help the reader why i'm doing this well anyway. heading as well could be better - why not just something straightforward and cheeky like "meditating on logs"
this is too many short sentences. we're going to take away the asd-ste-100 constraint. instead these review processes should help with converging onto a style that is native to me.

all across the post - you're using "raj" again and again - a lot of times. doesn't feel right when being read - i'm looking for more of a technical publishing journal vibe for a laboratory. this is more of a very robotic memoir.
too many short sections isn't looking good.
